selection: wealth concentration reasons that cause costs
description: The most relevant reasons why wealth concentration causes costs, each linked to wealth concentration with 'can cause' and quantified by the studies that report it for the world and per country: the lower growth of the GDP (OECD 2014 by Cingano, Ostry, Berg & Tsangarides 2014), the tax evasion of the richest households through offshore wealth (Zucman 2013, Alstadsæter, Johannesen & Zucman 2019, EU Tax Observatory 2024), the tax avoidance with the very low effective tax rates of the billionaires (EU Tax Observatory 2024), the political capture of the policy by the economic elites (Gilens & Page 2014), the low economic mobility across the generations (OECD 2014, Corak 2013) and the excess mortality (Kondo et al. 2009). The wealth shares of the World Inequality Report 2022 and the growth of the billionaire wealth (EU Tax Observatory 2024, Oxfam 2025) are added as the context of the reasons; they describe the concentration itself, so they do not carry a '<reason> due to wealth concentration' triple. The annual damage of wealth concentration and its solutions are stated in problem_wealth_concentration.json instead, because they are the row of the global problem ranking of the start page. Every number is taken from the named source as reported; a country that a study does not report is left out and never estimated. A share is stored as the decimal ratio, a loss as a positive number and a change with its sign. Each study has its own definition and metric: the growth, mobility and health studies measure the income inequality, which is the closest measured proxy of the wealth concentration, and the OECD finds that the gap between the low incomes and the rest drives the growth loss, not the pulling away of the top; so numbers of different studies are not comparable without reading the source description. Every amount of money is stated in euro: the US dollar figure of the source is converted with the ECB 2023 annual average of 1.0813 USD per EUR (the value of GDP.json) whatever the price base year of the source, and the source figure is kept in the description of the value. A value of a reason carries the triple '<reason> due to wealth concentration' and not the phrase 'wealth concentration' itself, because a value that names a global problem directly is a row of the global problem ranking of the start page, where only the potential loss and the solution of a problem belong.

sources.name: World Inequality Report 2022
sources.description: Chancel, L., Piketty, T., Saez, E., Zucman, G. et al. (2022): World Inequality Report 2022, World Inequality Lab, executive summary: the richest 10 percent of the global population own 76 percent of all wealth and the poorest half 2 percent; the richest 10 percent take 52 percent of the global income and the poorest half 8.5 percent; the top 1 percent took 38 percent of all additional wealth accumulated since the mid-1990s; the share of the global wealth of the billionaires rose from 1 percent in 1995 to over 3 percent; the wealth of the richest individuals grew at 6 to 9 percent per year since 1995, the average wealth at 3.2 percent per year.

sources.name: OECD (2014) Focus on Inequality and Growth
sources.description: OECD (2014): Focus on Inequality and Growth, December 2014, contact Federico Cingano, summary of Cingano, F. (2014): Trends in Income Inequality and its Impact on Economic Growth, OECD Social, Employment and Migration Working Papers No. 163, DOI 10.1787/5jxrjncwxv6j-en. A rise of the income inequality by 3 Gini points, the average increase in the OECD over the past two decades, drags down the economic growth by 0.35 percentage point per year for 25 years, a cumulated loss of the GDP of 8.5 percent at the end of the period; the rise of the inequality 1985-2005 knocked more than 10 percentage points off the cumulative growth 1990-2010 of the GDP per capita in Mexico and New Zealand, nearly 9 points in the United Kingdom, Finland and Norway and between 6 and 7 points in the United States, Italy and Sweden; the gap between the bottom four deciles and the rest drives the effect, no evidence is found that the pulling away of the high incomes harms growth; a 6 points higher income inequality (the US-Canada difference in 2010) lowers the numeracy of the individuals with a low parental education background by around 6 points, nearly 40 percent of the gap to the medium background.

sources.name: Ostry, Berg & Tsangarides (2014)
sources.description: Ostry, J. D., Berg, A., Tsangarides, C. G. (2014): Redistribution, Inequality, and Growth. IMF Staff Discussion Note SDN/14/02. An increase of the net Gini from 37 (the United States in 2005) to 42 (Gabon in 2005) decreases the growth on average by 0.5 percentage points, from 5 to 4.5 percent per year, holding the redistribution and the initial income constant; a one-Gini-point increase of the inequality is associated with a 6 percentage point higher risk that a growth spell ends the next year, i.e. a decrease of the expected spell length of about 7 percent; the redistribution itself does not lower the growth unless it is already very high.

sources.name: Zucman (2013)
sources.description: Zucman, G. (2013): The Missing Wealth of Nations: Are Europe and the U.S. net Debtors or net Creditors? Quarterly Journal of Economics 128(3), 1321-1364. Abstract: around 8 percent of the global financial wealth of the households is held in tax havens, three-quarters of which goes unrecorded.

sources.name: Alstadsæter, Johannesen & Zucman (2019)
sources.description: Alstadsæter, A., Johannesen, N., Zucman, G. (2019): Tax Evasion and Inequality. American Economic Review 109(6), 2073-2103. Leaked customer lists of offshore financial institutions matched to the administrative wealth records of Norway, Sweden and Denmark: the offshore tax evasion is highly concentrated among the rich; the 0.01 percent richest households evade about 25 percent of their taxes, while the tax evasion detected in stratified random tax audits is less than 5 percent throughout the distribution.

sources.name: EU Tax Observatory (2023) Global Tax Evasion Report 2024
sources.description: Alstadsæter, A., Godar, S., Nicolaides, P., Zucman, G. (2023): Global Tax Evasion Report 2024, EU Tax Observatory, October 2023. USD 12 trillion, the equivalent of 12 percent of the world GDP, was held offshore by households at the end of 2022 (financial assets only, reported and unreported); thanks to the automatic exchange of bank information the offshore tax evasion has declined by a factor of about three in less than 10 years and in the central scenario only about 25 percent of the offshore wealth evades taxation; the global billionaires have effective personal tax rates equivalent to 0 to 0.5 percent of their wealth, closer to 0.5 percent in the United States and closer to 0 percent in France; the wealth of the global billionaires has grown at 7 percent a year on average since 1995 net of inflation; a minimum tax of 2 percent of the wealth of the about 2'500 billionaires with close to USD 13 trillion would raise nearly USD 250 billion per year.

sources.name: Gilens & Page (2014)
sources.description: Gilens, M., Page, B. I. (2014): Testing Theories of American Politics: Elites, Interest Groups, and Average Citizens. Perspectives on Politics 12(3), 564-581. 1'779 policy issues of the United States: the economic elites and the organised business groups have substantial independent impacts on the policy, while the average citizens and the mass-based interest groups have little or no independent influence; in the multivariate model 4 the logit coefficient of the preferences of the economic elites (90th income percentile) is 0.76 and the one of the average citizens (50th income percentile) is 0.03 and not significant. The coefficients are taken from the reprint of the table in Bashir, O. S. (2015): Testing Inferences about American Politics: A Review of the 'Oligarchy' Result, Research and Politics, DOI 10.1177/2053168015608896, who argues that the high correlation of the two preferences makes the near-zero coefficient of the average citizens too likely to be produced by chance.

sources.name: Corak (2013)
sources.description: Corak, M. (2013): Income Inequality, Equality of Opportunity, and Intergenerational Mobility. Journal of Economic Perspectives 27(3), 79-102. The Great Gatsby Curve: the countries with more inequality also have less earnings mobility across the generations; in Finland, Norway and Denmark less than one-fifth of any economic advantage or disadvantage of a father is passed on to his son, in Italy, the United Kingdom and the United States roughly 50 percent; the American intergenerational earnings elasticity at about 0.5 is twice as high as the Canadian; the curve is a correlation, not a causal estimate.

sources.name: Kondo et al. (2009)
sources.description: Kondo, N., Sembajwe, G., Kawachi, I., van Dam, R. M., Subramanian, S. V., Yamagata, Z. (2009): Income inequality, mortality, and self rated health: meta-analysis of multilevel studies. BMJ 339, b4471. The cohort relative risk of mortality per 0.05 unit increase of the Gini coefficient is 1.08 (95 percent confidence interval 1.06 to 1.10), stronger above a Gini of 0.3; if the relation is causal, upwards of 1.5 million deaths or 9.6 percent of the adult mortality could be averted in 30 OECD countries by levelling the Gini coefficient below 0.3; the excess risks are 3 percent in Japan, 11 percent in the United States and 38 percent in Mexico.

sources.name: Oxfam (2025) Takers not Makers
sources.description: Taneja, A., Kamande, A., Guharay Gomez, C., Abed, D., Lawson, M., Mukhia, N. (2025): Takers not Makers: The unjust poverty and unearned wealth of colonialism. Oxfam International, 20 January 2025, an advocacy report based on the Forbes billionaire estimates: the billionaire wealth rose three times faster in 2024 than in 2023, by USD 2 trillion to USD 15 trillion with 2'769 billionaires (the amounts as reported by Al Jazeera on 20 January 2025); 60 percent of the billionaire wealth comes from inheritance, cronyism and corruption or monopoly power.
